sections.heading: Glomerular hematuria, nephritic syndrome and rapidly progressive GN: work-up and treatment
sections.html:
Recognise glomerular bleeding

Hematuria is glomerular when red cells are dysmorphic (acanthocytes), when there are red cell casts, or when it comes with proteinuria, hypertension or a rising creatinine. Glomerular hematuria needs a nephrology work-up rather than cystoscopy first. A patient whose creatinine is rising over days to weeks with an active sediment has rapidly progressive GN until proven otherwise, which is a medical emergency.

First tests

  • Urinalysis with microscopy; spot urine protein-to-creatinine (or albumin-to-creatinine) ratio; serum creatinine and electrolytes.
  • Serology chosen by the picture: C3 and C4; ANA and anti-dsDNA; ANCA (MPO and PR3 by immunoassay); anti-GBM antibody; anti-streptolysin O and anti-DNase B; hepatitis B and C, HIV; cryoglobulins and rheumatoid factor; serum protein electrophoresis with free light chains in older adults.
  • Kidney biopsy is the most accurate test and also grades activity and chronicity. In suspected rapidly progressive GN, start treatment without waiting for biopsy when serology is positive and the patient is deteriorating.

Treatment by disease

DiseaseManagement
Post-streptococcal GNSupportive: sodium and fluid restriction, loop diuretic for edema and hypertension, other antihypertensives as needed; antibiotics only for persisting streptococcal infection. Immunosuppression is not used. Persistently low C3 after about 8 weeks suggests another diagnosis (for example C3 glomerulopathy or lupus).
IgA nephropathySupportive care is the base: ACE inhibitor or ARB titrated to the highest tolerated dose, blood pressure control, an SGLT2 inhibitor when eGFR allows, and lifestyle measures; aim to lower proteinuria well below 1 g/day. Patients with persistent proteinuria at high risk of progression are considered for glucocorticoid-based or newer targeted therapies.
Anti-GBM diseasePlasma exchange to remove the antibody, plus glucocorticoids and cyclophosphamide, started urgently. Patients who need dialysis at presentation and have crescents in nearly all glomeruli rarely recover kidney function unless they have lung hemorrhage that needs treatment anyway.
ANCA-associated GNInduction with glucocorticoids plus rituximab or cyclophosphamide; the C5a receptor blocker avacopan can reduce glucocorticoid exposure; plasma exchange may be added for very severe kidney failure or anti-GBM overlap. Maintenance with rituximab (or azathioprine). Screen for and prevent Pneumocystis infection.
Lupus nephritis III or IV (± V)Glucocorticoids plus mycophenolate or low-dose IV cyclophosphamide, with add-on belimumab or a calcineurin inhibitor (voclosporin) in many patients; hydroxychloroquine for every patient with lupus unless contraindicated; ACE inhibitor or ARB for proteinuria. Mycophenolate is teratogenic: use effective contraception and switch to azathioprine before a planned pregnancy.
Cryoglobulinemic GN (hepatitis C)Direct-acting antivirals; rituximab, with plasma exchange for severe disease.

Indications for kidney biopsy in lupus

Biopsy a patient with lupus who has proteinuria of about 0.5 g/day or more, an active sediment (dysmorphic red cells, red cell casts) or an unexplained rise in creatinine. The class decides treatment, so it is not skipped.

Exam trap: a smoker with hemoptysis and kidney failure may have anti-GBM disease or ANCA vasculitis, and some patients have both antibodies. Send both serologies, and do not delay plasma exchange and immunosuppression while waiting for biopsy if the patient is deteriorating.

sections.heading: Nephrotic syndrome and interstitial nephritis: diagnosis, treatment and complications
sections.html:
Confirm and characterise

  • Quantify proteinuria with a spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (about 3–3.5 g/g or more is nephrotic range); 24-hour collection is rarely needed.
  • Check albumin, lipids, creatinine, glucose and hemoglobin A1c, and the secondary-cause panel: hepatitis B and C, HIV, ANA, complement, serum and urine protein electrophoresis with free light chains, and anti-PLA2R antibody.
  • Children aged about 1 to 10 years with typical nephrotic syndrome (normal complement, no gross hematuria, normal kidney function and blood pressure) are presumed to have minimal change disease and given oral glucocorticoids without biopsy; biopsy is for steroid resistance or atypical features.
  • Adults usually need a biopsy. An exception: a typical adult with nephrotic syndrome, preserved function and a positive anti-PLA2R antibody can be diagnosed with primary membranous nephropathy without biopsy.

General measures for any nephrotic patient

  • Dietary sodium restriction and a loop diuretic for edema (higher doses are often needed because the diuretic is protein bound in urine and less albumin carries it to the kidney).
  • ACE inhibitor or ARB to lower intraglomerular pressure and proteinuria, with blood pressure control.
  • Statin for persistent hyperlipidemia when the disease is not expected to remit soon.
  • Prophylactic anticoagulation is considered when albumin is very low (for example below about 2.0–2.5 g/dL), especially with membranous nephropathy and low bleeding risk; established venous thrombosis is treated with full anticoagulation.
  • Pneumococcal and seasonal influenza vaccination.

Disease-specific treatment

DiseaseTreatment
Minimal changeGlucocorticoids (most remit within weeks); for frequent relapses or steroid dependence, steroid-sparing agents such as rituximab, calcineurin inhibitors or cyclophosphamide. Stop an offending NSAID; look for lymphoma in an adult with suggestive features.
Primary FSGSSupportive care plus high-dose glucocorticoids; calcineurin inhibitor if resistant. Secondary FSGS is treated by addressing the cause (antiretroviral therapy for HIV-associated nephropathy, weight loss, stopping heroin or lithium) with RAS blockade; immunosuppression does not help secondary or genetic forms.
MembranousSupportive care for low-risk disease, since about a third remit spontaneously; rituximab (or cyclophosphamide with glucocorticoids, or a calcineurin inhibitor) for moderate to high risk. Anti-PLA2R levels track response. For PLA2R-negative disease in an older adult, look for a secondary cause, including age-appropriate cancer screening.
Diabetic kidney diseaseACE inhibitor or ARB, SGLT2 inhibitor, and in type 2 diabetes with persistent albuminuria a nonsteroidal mineralocorticoid antagonist (finerenone) and a GLP-1 receptor agonist with proven kidney benefit (see the CKD section).
AL amyloidosisConfirm with tissue (fat-pad or kidney biopsy with Congo red) and typing; treat the plasma cell clone.

Renal vein thrombosis

Suspect it in a nephrotic patient (classically membranous) with sudden flank pain, gross hematuria, a rise in creatinine, a raised LDH or an unexplained pulmonary embolism. Confirm with CT or MR venography (Doppler ultrasonography is an alternative), and anticoagulate.

Acute interstitial nephritis

Suspect AIN with a rising creatinine after a new drug, especially with pyuria, white cell casts, rash, fever or eosinophilia. The first step is to stop the likely drug. If creatinine does not improve within several days, or the injury is severe, confirm with biopsy and give glucocorticoids. Checkpoint-inhibitor AIN is treated with glucocorticoids and holding the drug.

Exam trap: a 4-year-old with new nephrotic syndrome and normal complement does not need a biopsy first. Start prednisone, and biopsy only if there is no remission.

furtherReading.label: StatPearls: Allergic and Drug-Induced Interstitial Nephritis

sections.heading: Renal cysts and benign masses: evaluation and management
sections.html:
The incidental renal cyst

Cysts found on CT or ultrasound done for another reason are classified by their CT (or MRI) features, using the Bosniak classification, which estimates the chance of malignancy.

ClassFeaturesAction
IThin smooth wall, no septa, calcification or solid parts, water density, no enhancementBenign: no follow-up
IIA few thin septa, fine calcification, or a small uniformly high-density nonenhancing cystBenign: no follow-up
IIFMore numerous or minimally thickened septa or wall; no measurable enhancing noduleImaging surveillance ("F" for follow-up) over several years
IIIThickened, irregular, enhancing walls or septaSurgical excision (often partial nephrectomy) or, for small cysts or frail patients, active surveillance
IVEnhancing soft-tissue nodule within the cystTreat as cancer: partial or radical nephrectomy (surveillance only if surgery is a poor option)

Ultrasound alone can confirm a simple cyst. An indeterminate lesion on ultrasound needs renal-protocol CT or MRI with contrast. Biopsy is rarely needed for cysts.

ADPKD: diagnosis

  • With a family history, ultrasound is the usual test. In families of unknown genotype, the number of cysts that confirms the diagnosis rises with age (for example, at least 3 cysts in total between 15 and 39 years; at least 2 in each kidney between 40 and 59 years). A normal ultrasound after 40 essentially excludes the disease. MRI is more sensitive in younger relatives being considered as kidney donors, and genetic testing settles unclear cases.
  • Total kidney volume (from MRI or CT) predicts the rate of decline and identifies rapid progressors.

ADPKD: management

  • Blood pressure: an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker first line (the RAAS is the driver). In younger patients with preserved GFR, a lower target (around 110/75 mm Hg) slows kidney growth if tolerated.
  • Fluids and salt: generous water intake (to suppress vasopressin) and dietary sodium restriction; avoid nephrotoxins such as NSAIDs.
  • Tolvaptan (vasopressin V2 receptor antagonist) for adults at risk of rapidly progressive disease (for example, large total kidney volume for age, or a fast fall in eGFR). It causes polyuria, thirst and nocturia, and it can cause serious liver injury, so liver tests are checked regularly, most closely in the first 18 months.
  • Pain and bleeding: most cyst hemorrhage settles with rest, fluids and analgesia (avoid NSAIDs when GFR is reduced).
  • Cyst infection: fever and focal pain, sometimes with negative urine cultures. Diagnose with imaging (MRI, or PET-CT when unclear) and treat for several weeks with a lipid-soluble antibiotic that enters cysts, such as a fluoroquinolone or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole; drain large infected cysts that do not respond.
  • Intracranial aneurysm screening: offer MR angiography to patients with a family history of aneurysm or subarachnoid hemorrhage, a prior rupture, a high-risk job (for example, pilots) or before major elective surgery. Routine screening of everyone is not recommended.
  • Kidney failure: dialysis or transplant; native nephrectomy if kidneys are so large they leave no room for the graft or cause recurrent bleeding or infection.

Benign solid masses

  • Angiomyolipoma: macroscopic fat on CT is diagnostic. Small asymptomatic tumours are watched with imaging. Treatment (selective arterial embolisation, nephron-sparing surgery or an mTOR inhibitor in tuberous sclerosis) is considered for symptoms, growth, large size or in women planning pregnancy. Acute retroperitoneal hemorrhage with shock is treated with resuscitation and emergency selective arterial embolisation, which stops bleeding while sparing kidney tissue.
  • Oncocytoma: a central scar on imaging is suggestive but not reliable; biopsy can suggest it, but because it can resemble chromophobe carcinoma, most enhancing solid masses are managed as possible cancer.

Exam trap: a sudden severe headache in a young adult with ADPKD is a ruptured berry aneurysm until proved otherwise: noncontrast CT head first.

sections.heading: Hematuria evaluation and management of kidney and bladder cancer
sections.html:
Hematuria: the work-up

  1. Confirm: a positive dipstick also reacts to myoglobin and free hemoglobin, so confirm with urine microscopy. Microscopic hematuria is 3 or more red cells per high-power field on a properly collected specimen.
  2. Look for benign or glomerular causes: infection (treat and repeat), menstruation, vigorous exercise or recent instrumentation (repeat later); dysmorphic red cells, red cell casts, proteinuria or a rising creatinine point to glomerular disease and nephrology referral rather than urologic imaging.
  3. Gross hematuria without an obvious benign cause, even once and even on anticoagulants, needs multiphase CT urography and cystoscopy.
  4. Microscopic hematuria is risk-stratified (age, sex, smoking, degree of hematuria, other risk factors). High-risk patients (for example older smokers or more than 25 red cells per high-power field) get CT urography and cystoscopy; low-risk patients (for example a young nonsmoking woman with 3–10 red cells) may be rechecked with a repeat urinalysis or evaluated after shared decision-making with cystoscopy and renal ultrasonography.

The solid renal mass

  • Characterise with renal-protocol CT or MRI (with contrast): enhancement means a solid tumour, fat means angiomyolipoma. Stage with chest imaging.
  • Localised small masses (up to about 4 cm, T1a): partial (nephron-sparing) nephrectomy is preferred, because preserving kidney function lowers later CKD and cardiovascular risk. Thermal ablation or active surveillance suits older or frail patients; biopsy helps when the result would change management.
  • Larger or central tumours, or renal vein involvement: radical nephrectomy, with thrombectomy for a vena caval thrombus.
  • After nephrectomy for clear cell RCC at high risk of recurrence, adjuvant pembrolizumab is an option.
  • Metastatic clear cell RCC: first-line systemic therapy is an immune checkpoint inhibitor-based combination (a PD-1 inhibitor with a VEGF receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitor, or nivolumab with ipilimumab). Conventional chemotherapy and hormonal therapy do not work.
  • VHL disease: lifelong surveillance (abdominal MRI, eye examination, brain and spine MRI, plasma metanephrines); small renal tumours are watched and removed with nephron-sparing surgery once they reach about 3 cm; belzutifan is an option for VHL tumours that do not need immediate surgery.

Bladder cancer

  • Transurethral resection of bladder tumour (TURBT) diagnoses, stages (it must sample detrusor muscle) and treats non-invasive disease.
  • Non-muscle-invasive, low risk: TURBT, often with one immediate post-resection instillation of intravesical chemotherapy, then surveillance cystoscopy.
  • Non-muscle-invasive, high grade or carcinoma in situ: TURBT (repeat resection for T1 tumours) followed by intravesical BCG induction and maintenance. Radical cystectomy if BCG fails.
  • Muscle-invasive (T2 or higher), no metastases: cisplatin-based neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by radical cystectomy with urinary diversion; bladder-sparing trimodality therapy (maximal TURBT with chemoradiation) is an alternative for selected patients.
  • Upper-tract urothelial carcinoma: CT urography and ureteroscopy with biopsy; usually nephroureterectomy, with endoscopic treatment for small low-grade tumours. Test for Lynch syndrome when appropriate.

Wilms tumour

  • An abdominal mass in a young child: abdominal ultrasonography first (solid versus cystic, kidney versus adrenal, renal vein and caval involvement), then CT or MRI of the abdomen and CT of the chest. Avoid repeated palpation, which can rupture the capsule.
  • Treatment combines nephrectomy and chemotherapy (plus radiation for advanced stages); cure rates are high for favourable histology.
  • Surveillance in Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome and other high-risk syndromes: abdominal (renal) ultrasonography every 3 months until about age 7; in Beckwith-Wiedemann, alpha-fetoprotein is also checked in early childhood for hepatoblastoma.

Exam trap: hematuria in a patient taking warfarin or a DOAC is still worked up fully; anticoagulation unmasks lesions, it does not explain them.

sections.heading: Approach to hematuria, proteinuria and abnormal urine output
sections.html:
Hematuria: confirm, exclude benign causes, then stratify

  1. Confirm a positive dipstick with microscopy. Microscopic hematuria is 3 or more red cells per high-power field on a properly collected specimen; a dipstick alone is not enough to start an evaluation.
  2. Exclude benign or transient causes: menstruation, vigorous exercise, recent instrumentation, sexual activity and urinary infection. Treat an infection and repeat the urinalysis afterwards.
  3. Look for a glomerular source: dysmorphic red cells, red cell casts, proteinuria, rising creatinine or new hypertension point to the kidney; refer to nephrology (urologic evaluation may still be needed if risk is high).
  4. Stratify risk of urothelial cancer in nonglomerular hematuria. Risk rises with age, male sex, smoking (pack-years), the number of red cells per field and a history of gross hematuria. Other risk factors: occupational exposure to aromatic amines or benzene dyes, cyclophosphamide, pelvic radiation, aristolochic acid, chronic catheter.
Risk group (AUA microhematuria guidance)Typical featuresEvaluation
LowYounger women and men, little or no smoking, 3–10 red cells per field, no other risk factorsShared decision: repeat urinalysis within about 6 months, or cystoscopy with renal ultrasonography
IntermediateMiddle age, moderate smoking, 11–25 red cells per field, or persistent low-risk hematuriaCystoscopy and renal ultrasonography
HighAge 60 years or older, more than 30 pack-years, more than 25 red cells per field, or any gross hematuriaCystoscopy and CT urography (multiphase CT with an excretory phase)

Gross hematuria without an obvious benign cause (for example, a clear infection that resolves) needs cystoscopy and CT urography in adults, even if it happened once. Anticoagulation does not explain hematuria: patients on anticoagulants are evaluated in the same way. If contrast cannot be given, use MR urography or noncontrast imaging with retrograde pyelography.

Proteinuria: quantify and classify

  • A positive dipstick is followed by a quantitative spot ratio (UACR for albuminuria in diabetes and chronic kidney disease, UPCR when overall protein matters). Categories of albuminuria: A1 below 30, A2 30–300 and A3 above 300 mg/g.
  • Repeat a positive test: transient proteinuria from fever, exercise or acute illness disappears.
  • In adolescents and young adults with low-grade proteinuria, normal blood pressure and normal kidney function, check a first-morning sample (or a split collection of upright and recumbent urine). Protein only when upright is orthostatic proteinuria, which is benign and needs reassurance and perhaps a recheck.
  • Persistent proteinuria: serum creatinine and eGFR, urine microscopy, blood pressure, glucose and A1c, and, depending on the context, serum and urine protein electrophoresis with free light chains (age over 40, anemia, hypercalcemia), complement, ANA, hepatitis B and C, HIV. Nephrotic-range protein, active sediment or falling eGFR prompt nephrology referral and often biopsy.

Oliguria and acute retention

In any patient with a sudden fall in urine output, first rule out obstruction: bladder scan or straight catheterisation (post-void residual above about 200 mL suggests retention), and flush or replace an existing catheter. Common causes in older men are prostatic enlargement, anticholinergic or opioid drugs and constipation. After relief of prolonged obstruction, watch for a post-obstructive diuresis (urine output above about 200 mL/h) with losses of sodium, potassium and water. Only then pursue prerenal and intrinsic causes (see acute kidney injury).

Red or dark urine with few red cells

  • Rhabdomyolysis: heme-positive dipstick, few red cells, creatine kinase often above about 5 times normal (often far higher), hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, early hypocalcemia. Treat with early, generous isotonic fluids aiming at high urine output; stop the offending drug.
  • Intravascular hemolysis: pink plasma, low haptoglobin, high LDH, hemoglobinuria; for example G6PD deficiency after an oxidant drug.

Exam trap: a patient taking warfarin or a direct oral anticoagulant who develops hematuria still gets the full evaluation. Anticoagulation unmasks lesions; it rarely causes bleeding from a normal urinary tract.

sections.heading: Acute kidney injury: evaluation and management
sections.html:
Definition and staging (KDIGO)

AKI is any of: serum creatinine up by at least 0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours; creatinine at least 1.5 times baseline within the prior 7 days; or urine output below 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 hours.

StageCreatinineUrine output
11.5–1.9 × baseline, or rise of at least 0.3 mg/dLBelow 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6–12 hours
22.0–2.9 × baselineBelow 0.5 mL/kg/h for 12 hours or more
33 × baseline, or creatinine 4.0 mg/dL or more, or start of kidney replacement therapyBelow 0.3 mL/kg/h for 24 hours or more, or anuria for 12 hours or more

First steps in every case

  1. Review the history and medicines: volume losses, hypotension, contrast, nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, vancomycin with piperacillin-tazobactam), ACE inhibitors, ARBs and diuretics.
  2. Assess volume status at the bedside.
  3. Urinalysis with microscopy (casts, cells, crystals), urine sodium, creatinine and urea for fractional excretion.
  4. Check for obstruction: bladder scan or catheter for retention; renal ultrasound for hydronephrosis.
  5. Check potassium, bicarbonate and calcium/phosphate; review drug doses for the current GFR.

By cause

  • Prerenal from volume loss: isotonic crystalloid; creatinine should improve within 24–72 hours. In heart failure or cirrhosis, "prerenal" means low effective volume; treat the cause (diuresis for congestion, albumin and vasoconstrictors for hepatorenal syndrome).
  • ATN: supportive; keep euvolemia, stop nephrotoxins, adjust doses, avoid hyperkalemia, and wait for recovery over 1–3 weeks.
  • Postrenal: relieve the obstruction (urethral catheter for bladder outlet obstruction; stent or nephrostomy for ureteral obstruction). Watch for post-obstructive diuresis.
  • Rhabdomyolysis: early, generous isotonic fluids aiming for a high urine output; treat hyperkalemia; avoid giving calcium for asymptomatic hypocalcemia, which often rebounds during recovery.
  • Tumor lysis syndrome: prevent in high-risk patients with IV fluids and rasburicase (converts uric acid to soluble allantoin; contraindicated in G6PD deficiency); allopurinol for intermediate risk.
  • Contrast-associated AKI: in people at high risk (low eGFR), give isotonic IV fluid before and after contrast and stop nephrotoxins; do not withhold an indicated contrast study for fear of AKI alone.

When to start dialysis urgently

Dialysis is started for complications that do not respond to medical treatment:

  • severe metabolic acidosis;
  • hyperkalemia not controlled medically;
  • dialysable poisons (methanol, ethylene glycol, lithium, salicylates);
  • volume overload with pulmonary edema despite diuretics;
  • uremic complications: pericarditis, encephalopathy, uremic bleeding.

A creatinine or BUN number alone is not an indication.

Exam trap: a pericardial friction rub in a patient with advanced kidney failure is uremic pericarditis, an indication for urgent dialysis. NSAIDs and colchicine, the usual pericarditis treatments, are not the answer.

sections.heading: Chronic kidney disease: staging, slowing progression and treating complications
sections.html:
Staging (KDIGO): cause, GFR and albuminuria

GFR categoryeGFR (mL/min/1.73 m²)
G190 or more (with kidney damage)
G260–89 (with kidney damage)
G3a45–59
G3b30–44
G415–29
G5Below 15 (kidney failure)

Albuminuria by urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR): A1 below 30 mg/g, A2 30–300 mg/g, A3 above 300 mg/g. Risk rises with both lower GFR and higher ACR, so both are reported (for example "G3a A3"). Confirm abnormal ACR on repeat testing. Screen people with diabetes and hypertension yearly with eGFR and ACR.

Slowing progression

  • Blood pressure: KDIGO suggests a systolic target below 120 mm Hg when tolerated, measured in a standardised way.
  • ACE inhibitor or ARB (one, not both) at the highest tolerated dose for albuminuria (especially A3, and A2 with diabetes). Check creatinine and potassium after starting; accept a creatinine rise up to about 30%.
  • SGLT2 inhibitor for type 2 diabetes with CKD and eGFR at least 20, and for CKD without diabetes when eGFR is at least 20 and ACR is at least 200 mg/g or heart failure is present. Continue it once started, even as eGFR falls, until dialysis.
  • Finerenone (nonsteroidal mineralocorticoid antagonist) in type 2 diabetes with persistent albuminuria despite maximal ACE inhibitor or ARB, if eGFR is at least 25 and potassium is normal.
  • GLP-1 receptor agonist for glycemic control in type 2 diabetes with CKD when more is needed beyond metformin and SGLT2 inhibitors.
  • Statin for adults 50 years and older with CKD; stop smoking; avoid NSAIDs; dose-adjust drugs (metformin is reduced at eGFR below 45 and stopped below 30).

Treating complications

ComplicationApproach
AnemiaExclude other causes; replete iron first (ferritin and transferrin saturation; IV iron is often needed). An erythropoiesis-stimulating agent (ESA) is considered for persistent hemoglobin below 10 g/dL; avoid targeting normal hemoglobin (13 g/dL or more), which raises stroke and thrombosis risk
Mineral and bone disorderLower phosphate (diet, then phosphate binders); correct vitamin D deficiency; for progressive secondary hyperparathyroidism, calcitriol or a calcimimetic (cinacalcet); parathyroidectomy for refractory or tertiary disease
Metabolic acidosisOral sodium bicarbonate when serum bicarbonate is persistently low (below about 18 mEq/L)
HyperkalemiaLow-potassium diet; stop potassium-raising drugs that are not essential; loop or thiazide diuretic; potassium binders (patiromer, sodium zirconium cyclosilicate) to keep RAS blockade going
Volume overload, edemaSodium restriction and loop diuretics

Planning kidney replacement

Refer to nephrology at eGFR below 30 (or earlier for heavy albuminuria or rapid decline). At G4, discuss the options: transplant (best survival; preemptive transplant before dialysis is ideal), hemodialysis (create an arteriovenous fistula months ahead, and protect the non-dominant arm from venipuncture), peritoneal dialysis, or conservative care. Start dialysis for symptoms or complications, not at a fixed eGFR.

Exam trap: do not combine an ACE inhibitor with an ARB; dual blockade raises hyperkalemia and AKI without renal benefit.

sections.heading: Nephrolithiasis: acute care, workup and prevention
sections.html:
Presentation

Sudden, colicky flank pain radiating to the groin, with nausea and hematuria (gross or microscopic). Pain does not ease with position, unlike peritonitis. Fever with a stone means possible infected obstruction.

Imaging

  • Noncontrast low-dose CT of the abdomen and pelvis is the most accurate test and shows size and location.
  • Ultrasound first in pregnancy and in children, and reasonable in young adults with a typical recurrent episode; it shows hydronephrosis even when it misses small ureteral stones.

Acute management

  • Analgesia: an NSAID (for example ketorolac) is first line when kidney function allows; add opioids if needed.
  • Stones up to 10 mm without complications: trial of passage with hydration and pain control. For distal ureteral stones 5–10 mm, an alpha blocker (tamsulosin) improves passage. Most stones under 5 mm pass on their own. Strain the urine and send the stone for analysis.
  • Urgent urology (decompression by stent or nephrostomy) for infection with obstruction, AKI, obstruction of a solitary or transplanted kidney, bilateral obstruction, or pain or vomiting that cannot be controlled.
  • Elective removal (ureteroscopy, shock wave lithotripsy, percutaneous nephrolithotomy for large or staghorn stones) for stones that do not pass in about 4–6 weeks or are too large to pass.

Workup after a stone

Everyone: stone analysis, serum calcium, creatinine, electrolytes and uric acid, and urinalysis. High-risk or recurrent stone formers (children, solitary kidney, multiple or recurrent stones, bowel disease): a 24-hour urine for volume, calcium, oxalate, citrate, uric acid, sodium and creatinine. A high serum calcium leads to PTH testing for primary hyperparathyroidism.

Prevention

FindingPrevention
Low urine volume (all types)Fluids for a urine output of at least 2.5 L/day
HypercalciuriaLow sodium intake, normal dietary calcium (do not restrict), limit animal protein; thiazide if stones recur
HypocitraturiaPotassium citrate
HyperoxaluriaLimit high-oxalate foods; calcium with meals; in enteric hyperoxaluria, low-fat diet and calcium supplements with meals
Uric acid stonesPotassium citrate to raise urine pH to about 6–6.5; allopurinol if hyperuricosuria persists
Calcium oxalate stones with hyperuricosuriaAllopurinol
CystineVery high fluid intake, alkalinisation, then tiopronin
StruviteComplete stone removal and treatment of infection

Exam trap: a low-calcium diet raises the risk of calcium oxalate stones, because less calcium is left in the gut to bind oxalate.

sections.heading: Renovascular disease: when to suspect it, imaging and treatment
sections.html:
When to suspect renovascular hypertension

  • Hypertension starting before about 30 years (think fibromuscular dysplasia, especially in women) or a new, severe or resistant hypertension after about 55 years.
  • A rise in serum creatinine of more than about 30% after starting an ACE inhibitor or ARB.
  • Recurrent "flash" pulmonary edema with preserved ejection fraction, or unexplained kidney atrophy or a size difference of more than about 1.5 cm between kidneys.
  • An abdominal or flank bruit, especially one with a diastolic component; diffuse atherosclerosis.
  • Hypokalemia with high renin and high aldosterone (contrast primary aldosteronism: high aldosterone with suppressed renin).

Imaging

TestUse
Renal artery duplex ultrasonographyNoninvasive first test in many centres; no contrast; operator dependent, limited by obesity and bowel gas
CT angiographyExcellent detail of the arteries and the beaded pattern of fibromuscular dysplasia; needs iodinated contrast
MR angiographyAlternative when iodinated contrast is undesirable; gadolinium is avoided in severe CKD (eGFR below 30) unless a lower-risk group II agent is used
Catheter angiographyReference standard; done when intervention is planned, with pressure gradients across the lesion

In fibromuscular dysplasia, image the arteries from head to pelvis once (CT angiography), because carotid, vertebral and other lesions and aneurysms are common.

Treatment

  • Atherosclerotic stenosis: medical therapy first: blood pressure control (an ACE inhibitor or ARB is appropriate in unilateral disease, with creatinine and potassium checked within 1–2 weeks), a high-intensity statin, antiplatelet therapy, smoking cessation and diabetes control. Large randomised trials found that adding stenting to optimal medical therapy did not reduce cardiovascular or renal events in typical patients. Revascularisation is considered for recurrent flash pulmonary edema, rapidly declining kidney function attributable to the stenosis, or truly refractory hypertension.
  • Fibromuscular dysplasia with hypertension: percutaneous transluminal angioplasty without a stent, which often improves or cures the hypertension, especially in younger patients with short-duration disease; antiplatelet therapy is commonly given.

Renal infarction

Suspect it in a patient with atrial fibrillation or another embolic source who has acute flank pain, hematuria and a high LDH, especially when a stone is not seen. Contrast-enhanced CT (CT angiography) shows a wedge-shaped perfusion defect; noncontrast CT for stones is normal. Treat with anticoagulation (heparin, then long-term oral anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation); catheter-directed therapy is reserved for selected early, complete occlusions.

Atheroembolic kidney disease

Kidney function that worsens over days to weeks after catheterisation, with livedo and eosinophilia, is atheroembolic disease, whereas contrast-associated injury appears within 24–72 hours and usually recovers within a week. Treatment is supportive: blood pressure control, statin, aspirin, avoidance of further arterial procedures and, if possible, anticoagulation; dialysis if needed. There is no proven role for glucocorticoids.

Scleroderma renal crisis

Abrupt hypertension (sometimes normotensive), rising creatinine and often microangiopathic hemolysis in a patient with early diffuse systemic sclerosis: start a short-acting ACE inhibitor (captopril) and titrate quickly, continuing it even when creatinine rises or dialysis is needed, because many patients recover enough to stop dialysis. Avoid high-dose glucocorticoids in at-risk patients. Prophylactic ACE inhibitors are not recommended.

Renal vein thrombosis

Diagnose with Doppler ultrasonography, CT or MR venography. Treat acute thrombosis with anticoagulation, continued while the nephrotic syndrome persists. In membranous nephropathy with serum albumin very low (well below about 2.5 g/dL) and low bleeding risk, prophylactic anticoagulation is sometimes considered.

Exam trap: in atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis the next step is almost always optimal medical therapy, not stenting. The question often hides one of the few revascularisation triggers, such as recurrent flash pulmonary edema.

sections.heading: Genitourinary trauma: evaluation and management
sections.html:
Initial approach

Genitourinary injuries are evaluated after the primary survey. Gross hematuria, a pelvic fracture, blood at the urethral meatus, flank bruising or penetrating injury near the kidneys or pelvis prompts imaging. Hemodynamic stability decides whether a patient goes to imaging or straight to the operating room.

Urethral injury

  • Suspect it with blood at the meatus, inability to void, perineal or scrotal (butterfly) hematoma or a high-riding prostate.
  • Do not pass a urethral catheter first. A retrograde urethrogram comes before any catheter, because blind catheterisation can turn a partial tear into a complete one.
  • If the urethrogram shows disruption, drain the bladder with a suprapubic cystostomy. Repair is delayed (urethroplasty months later) or done by early endoscopic realignment in selected patients. Late complications: stricture, erectile dysfunction, incontinence.

Bladder injury

  • Diagnosis: CT cystography (or conventional retrograde cystography) with the bladder fully distended through a catheter (about 300–350 mL of contrast in adults). Standard CT with passive filling misses ruptures.
  • Extraperitoneal rupture: contrast around the bladder base in a flame pattern. Most are managed with catheter drainage for about 2 weeks and a cystogram before removal. Operate if the bladder neck is involved, bone fragments lie in the bladder, or the abdomen is being opened anyway.
  • Intraperitoneal rupture: contrast outlines bowel loops and fills the paracolic gutters. It needs surgical repair, because urine keeps leaking into the peritoneum.

Kidney injury

  • Imaging: contrast CT with delayed (excretory) images, which show the collecting system and urine leak. Indications in adults: gross hematuria, microscopic hematuria with hypotension, or a mechanism or examination that suggests renal injury (rapid deceleration, flank wound, lower rib fractures).
  • Grading (AAST) runs from I (contusion or small subcapsular hematoma) to V (shattered kidney or avulsion of the hilum, or devascularised kidney with active bleeding).
  • Management: most injuries, including many high-grade ones in stable patients, are managed nonoperatively with bed rest, serial hemoglobin and observation. Active contrast extravasation or a pseudoaneurysm in a stable or transiently responsive patient is treated with angioembolisation. Persistent hemodynamic instability, an expanding or pulsatile hematoma at laparotomy, or hilar avulsion needs exploration. Urine leaks often seal; persistent ones get a ureteral stent.

Ureteral injury

Usually iatrogenic. Recognised during surgery, it is repaired at once. Recognised later, it shows as flank pain, fever, ileus, rising creatinine, or watery vaginal discharge (ureterovaginal fistula). CT urography or retrograde pyelography confirms it; a stent or percutaneous nephrostomy diverts urine while it heals or until repair.

Exam trap: in a pelvic fracture with blood at the meatus, the next step is a retrograde urethrogram, not a Foley catheter and not a CT of the abdomen.

sections.heading: Incontinence, neurogenic bladder, obstruction, reflux and prolapse: management
sections.html:
Urinary incontinence in practice

Start with history, a bladder diary, examination (including pelvic examination and cough stress test), urinalysis to exclude infection and hematuria, and a post-void residual when retention is possible. Look for reversible contributors: infection, atrophic vaginitis, drugs (diuretics, sedatives, anticholinergics, alpha blockers in women), constipation, excess fluid or caffeine, poor mobility and hyperglycemia.

TypeFirst lineNext steps
StressPelvic floor muscle training, weight lossVaginal pessary or urethral insert; midurethral sling; bulking agents
Urge (overactive bladder)Bladder training (scheduled, gradually lengthened voiding), fluid and caffeine adjustment, pelvic floor trainingBeta-3 agonist or antimuscarinic; then intradetrusor onabotulinumtoxinA, sacral neuromodulation or tibial nerve stimulation
MixedTreat the most bothersome part firstCombine approaches
OverflowTreat the cause (stop offending drugs, alpha blocker for prostatic obstruction)Clean intermittent catheterisation for an underactive detrusor
FunctionalPrompted or scheduled toileting, mobility aids, bedside commodeAddress cognition, environment and caregiving

In older adults, strongly anticholinergic drugs (oxybutynin especially) can cause confusion, constipation, dry mouth and falls, and add to the anticholinergic burden in dementia; a beta-3 agonist is preferred when a drug is needed. Mirabegron can raise blood pressure, so check it on treatment.

Neurogenic bladder

  • Underactive detrusor or large residual (spina bifida, cauda equina, diabetic neuropathy): clean intermittent catheterisation every 4–6 hours is preferred over an indwelling catheter.
  • Overactive detrusor with dyssynergia (spinal cord injury, multiple sclerosis): antimuscarinic or beta-3 agonist plus intermittent catheterisation; intradetrusor onabotulinumtoxinA if needed. Monitor kidney function and the upper tracts with ultrasound because of the high pressures.
  • Autonomic dysreflexia: sit the patient up, loosen tight clothing and look for the trigger, usually a blocked catheter or full bladder; drain it. Treat severe persistent hypertension with a fast-acting agent such as nitrates if there is no recent phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor use.

Obstruction

  • Acute urinary retention (often prostatic enlargement with an anticholinergic or decongestant trigger): drain with a urethral catheter (suprapubic if that fails), start an alpha-1 blocker, and attempt a trial without catheter after a few days.
  • Hydronephrosis on ultrasound with rising creatinine: find the level. Bilateral hydronephrosis with a distended bladder means outlet obstruction (catheter first); unilateral or bilateral hydronephrosis with an empty bladder means ureteral obstruction (stent or nephrostomy).
  • Post-obstructive diuresis: after decompression, monitor urine output, vital signs and electrolytes closely. Replace fluids with a hypotonic or isotonic solution at less than the urine output (for example about half), so as not to drive the diuresis.

Vesicoureteral reflux

Reflux of urine from bladder to ureter through an incompetent ureterovesical junction (primary: short intramural ureter; secondary: high bladder pressure from valves or neurogenic bladder). It predisposes to pyelonephritis and renal scarring. Graded I (ureter only) to V (gross dilation and tortuosity of the ureter and pelvis with blunted calyces) on voiding cystourethrography.

  • After a first febrile UTI in a child aged 2–24 months, obtain renal and bladder ultrasonography. Voiding cystourethrography follows if ultrasound shows hydronephrosis, scarring or other findings that suggest high-grade reflux or obstruction, or after a second febrile UTI.
  • Low grades often resolve with growth. Management includes treating bladder and bowel dysfunction (constipation), prompt treatment of febrile UTIs, continuous antibiotic prophylaxis for selected children (for example higher grades or recurrent infection), and surgery (ureteral reimplantation or endoscopic injection) for breakthrough infections, high grades that persist or new scarring.

Enuresis

  • Primary nocturnal enuresis (never dry, older than 5 years): reassurance, then a bed-wetting alarm (most durable) or oral desmopressin (restrict evening fluids to avoid hyponatremia).
  • Secondary enuresis (wetting again after at least 6 months dry): look for a cause: UTI, constipation, new-onset diabetes mellitus or diabetes insipidus (urinalysis for glucose and specific gravity), obstructive sleep apnea, psychosocial stress and, when suspected, abuse.

Other mechanical disorders

  • Urethral diverticulum (women): a tender anterior vaginal wall mass, post-void dribbling, dysuria, dyspareunia and recurrent UTI; pus may be expressed from the meatus. MRI of the pelvis is the most accurate test; symptomatic diverticula are excised.
  • Pelvic organ prolapse (cystocele, uterine or vaginal vault prolapse, rectocele): pressure, a vaginal bulge, voiding difficulty and incomplete emptying. Treat only if symptomatic: pelvic floor training, a pessary, or surgical repair. A large prolapse can kink the urethra and cause retention or even hydronephrosis.

sections.heading: Congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract: evaluation and management
sections.html:
Prenatal hydronephrosis

Dilation of the renal pelvis is the commonest anomaly found on prenatal ultrasonography. Most mild dilation resolves. After birth:

  • Unilateral hydronephrosis with a normal bladder: renal and bladder ultrasonography after about 48 hours of life (and within the first weeks). Earlier scans underestimate dilation because newborns are relatively oliguric in the first 1–2 days.
  • Bilateral hydronephrosis, a thick bladder or a dilated posterior urethra in a boy, or oligohydramnios: suspect posterior urethral valves. Scan in the first day, place a urethral catheter, and obtain voiding cystourethrography.
  • Persistent or worsening dilation leads to voiding cystourethrography (reflux, valves) and a diuretic renal scan (MAG3 with furosemide), which measures split function and drainage.

Ureteropelvic junction obstruction

  • Ultrasonography: dilated pelvis and calyces with a non-dilated ureter.
  • Diuretic renography: delayed drainage after furosemide indicates obstruction; split function is measured at the same time.
  • Many infants are watched with serial ultrasound. Pyeloplasty (open, laparoscopic or robotic dismembered pyeloplasty) is offered for symptoms (pain, infection, stones), reduced split function (often below about 40%), falling function on follow-up or worsening dilation.

Multicystic dysplastic kidney

Ultrasound shows noncommunicating cysts without normal parenchyma; a renal scan confirms no function. Management is conservative: serial ultrasonography to confirm involution and growth of the other kidney, and evaluation of the contralateral kidney, which has reflux or ureteropelvic junction obstruction in a meaningful share of children (voiding cystourethrography if it is dilated or the child has a febrile UTI). Nephrectomy is reserved for rare complications such as a large mass effect, hypertension or a solid component.

Bilateral agenesis and lethal oligohydramnios

Absent kidneys and bladder with anhydramnios at the mid-trimester anatomy scan predict lethal pulmonary hypoplasia. Counsel the family about the prognosis and the options (continuing with perinatal palliative care or ending the pregnancy), with support and genetic evaluation, because some forms recur.

Duplex systems and ectopic ureter

A girl who is wet all day and night yet also voids normally has an ectopic ureter until proven otherwise. Renal and bladder ultrasonography usually shows a duplex kidney with a dilated upper pole; MRI urography or cystoscopy locates the opening. Treatment is surgical (upper-pole heminephrectomy if that moiety does not function, or ureteral reimplantation or ureteroureterostomy). A ureterocele may be punctured endoscopically.

Horseshoe and pelvic kidney

Usually found incidentally and need no treatment. Children with Turner syndrome should have renal ultrasonography at diagnosis because of the frequent horseshoe kidney and collecting-system anomalies. Ectopic kidneys complicate trauma, abdominal aortic surgery and transplant surgery planning.

Urachal remnants

A newborn with persistent clear, urine-like drainage from the umbilicus may have a patent urachus; a fluid creatinine much higher than serum supports it. Ultrasonography of the umbilical region and bladder is the first test, with voiding cystourethrography to exclude bladder outlet obstruction, which can keep the urachus open. Symptomatic remnants are excised to prevent infection and later malignancy.

Bladder exstrophy

Diagnosed at birth (or prenatally by a non-visualised bladder with a low umbilical cord insertion). Cover the bladder plate with plastic wrap and refer for staged reconstruction; long-term issues are continence, fertility, upper-tract protection and cancer surveillance.

Exam trap: a newborn ultrasound on the first day after mild unilateral prenatal hydronephrosis can falsely reassure. Wait about 48 hours unless bilateral disease or a male infant with suspected valves needs earlier assessment.

sections.heading: Drug-induced kidney and urinary problems: recognition and management
sections.html:
Recognising drug-related kidney injury

Review every drug, including over-the-counter NSAIDs, proton pump inhibitors, supplements and recent contrast, whenever creatinine rises. The urine sediment and the time course usually point to the mechanism.

PatternTypical drugsCluesManagement
Hemodynamic (prerenal)NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors or ARBs, diuretics, calcineurin inhibitorsBland sediment, BUN:creatinine above 20, low urine sodium; often a volume-depleted older patientHold the offending drugs, restore volume, recheck
Acute tubular necrosisAminoglycosides, cisplatin, amphotericin B, contrastMuddy brown granular casts, urine sodium above 40 mEq/L, FENa above 2%; aminoglycoside injury is nonoliguric and appears after 5–10 daysStop or dose-adjust, monitor levels, replace magnesium and potassium, avoid other nephrotoxins
Acute interstitial nephritisBeta-lactams, PPIs, NSAIDs, sulfonamides, immune checkpoint inhibitorsSterile pyuria, white cell casts, sometimes rash, fever or eosinophiliaStop the drug; corticosteroids if no prompt recovery. For checkpoint inhibitors: hold the drug and start prednisone for moderate or worse injury
Crystal nephropathyIV acyclovir, methotrexate, sulfadiazine, indinavirCrystals in urine, AKI within days of a high doseHydrate, stop or reduce the drug; for methotrexate, leucovorin, alkalinisation and glucarpidase if severe
Pseudo-AKI (creatinine secretion blocked)Trimethoprim, cimetidine; some kinase inhibitorsCreatinine up about 10–30% within days, BUN unchanged, bland urine; cystatin C unchangedNo change needed if this is the only finding; watch potassium with trimethoprim

ACE inhibitors and ARBs: when a creatinine rise is acceptable

Check creatinine and potassium within about 2–4 weeks of starting or increasing the dose. A rise of up to about 30% that then stabilises is expected and the drug should be continued, because it reflects the intended fall in intraglomerular pressure. A larger rise calls for a search for volume depletion, NSAIDs or renal artery stenosis and dose reduction or a pause. Manage mild hyperkalemia with dietary advice, stopping potassium supplements, a diuretic or a potassium binder before abandoning the drug.

Iodinated contrast

  • Do not withhold a clinically necessary contrast study because of kidney function; the risk is small and mostly confined to eGFR below about 30 mL/min/1.73 m² (or AKI).
  • For high-risk patients who are not volume overloaded: IV isotonic crystalloid before and after, the lowest needed dose of a low- or iso-osmolar agent, and pausing NSAIDs and diuretics where safe.
  • N-acetylcysteine and prophylactic dialysis do not help. Metformin is held after contrast in patients with eGFR below 30 or AKI.

Gadolinium

In eGFR below 30 or dialysis, use a lower-risk (macrocyclic, group II) agent at the lowest dose only when the information is needed; for patients already on hemodialysis, dialysis soon after the scan is commonly arranged.

Specific drugs

  • Aminoglycosides: once-daily dosing, trough monitoring, shortest course; avoid with loop diuretics, vancomycin, contrast and NSAIDs where possible.
  • Cisplatin: prehydrate with saline and give magnesium. Hypomagnesemia makes hypokalemia refractory (magnesium normally restrains potassium secretion through ROMK), so replace magnesium first or together with potassium.
  • Lithium: monitor levels, creatinine, calcium and TSH. For nephrogenic DI when lithium must continue, add amiloride; thiazides also reduce polyuria but raise lithium levels.
  • Tenofovir: monitor creatinine, urine glucose and protein and phosphate on TDF; switch to tenofovir alafenamide or another regimen if tubulopathy appears.
  • Immune checkpoint inhibitors (pembrolizumab, nivolumab, ipilimumab): AIN is the usual kidney lesion, often weeks to months in and often with a PPI or NSAID as co-trigger. Exclude other causes, hold the inhibitor and give prednisone for moderate or worse injury; rechallenge may be possible once recovered, after discussion with oncology.
  • Cyclophosphamide/ifosfamide: hydration and mesna to prevent hemorrhagic cystitis; evaluate later hematuria for bladder cancer.

Drug-induced urinary retention

Suspect it in an older man with prostatic enlargement who has just started an antihistamine, antimuscarinic, tricyclic, decongestant or opioid, or after anesthesia. Confirm with a bladder scan (post-void residual). Decompress the bladder with a urethral catheter (suprapubic catheter if urethral placement fails or is contraindicated), stop the drug, and in men start an alpha-1 blocker such as tamsulosin before a trial without catheter.

Exam trap: a creatinine rise of about 0.2–0.3 mg/dL a few days after starting trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole with an unchanged BUN and bland urine is blocked creatinine secretion, not kidney injury. Stopping the antibiotic is not needed for that reason alone.
